items.title: Australia need a way to turn moments into momentum to revive spirits
items.desc:
The Wallabies have a squad capable of magic but doubts remain over whether their talents can be knitted into a great team

There are moments when Australia look like a team that can take on the world. Moments when they’re trailing by two in the 83rd minute at Twickenham and all of a sudden Len Ikitau has snapped an underhand pass through to Max Jorgensen and he’s haring down the wing to score in the corner. Moments when Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has ripped his way around Tom Curry, inside Bundee Aki, and over Tadhg Beirne, to send Tom Wright racing into the empty space of the British and Irish Lions backfield. Moments when they’re down to 11 men and defending a four-point lead with five to play against the Springboks, and somehow come out of it with a win.

And then there’s the rest of it. There’s never yet been a Wallabies team that didn’t have these flickers and sparks of ability in them, but it has been a long time since there has been one that could do it often enough, for long enough to win, and then all over again in the next Test and the one after. They lost all four Tests on tour in Europe last autumn, and two more in the summer besides. Then they went on an unbeaten run through six more against Italy, Japan, Argentina and South Africa before being knocked on to their backsides by the All Blacks in back-to-back defeats in the Bledisloe Cup, 31 points one week, 22 the next.

items.title: Injury crises and Borthwick under scrutiny: it’s that time of year again for England rugby
items.desc:
Sunday’s hosts need to stop looking for excuses and focus on what they can control to kick off the Nations Championship against battle-hardened Australia

Several things are increasingly guaranteed from an English rugby perspective around this time of year. Bang on cue the injury news and the weather both start to worsen. Cracks in the relationship between the players and their head coach, in this case Steve Borthwick, begin to surface. And as the crowds stream up from Twickenham railway station past the biltong and burger stalls, no one has much idea what to expect.

This year it has been the same old story. Particularly on the injury front. If Tom Curry, Alex Mitchell and Archie McParland had not all been hurt on the Bagshot training pitch, all three would probably be in England’s matchday 23. With Guy Pepper, Benhard van Rensburg, Sam Underhill, Kepu Tuipulotu and Chandler Cunningham-South also out of the running, the squad is not quite as fizzing with energy and dynamism as it might be.

items.title: Red Roses put defeats behind them by crushing USA to extend 35-year streak
items.desc:
• WXV: USA 12-55 England

  • Claudia Moloney-MacDonald runs in four tries

England have seen a lot of records crumble around them in this WXV Global Series but the world champions were not going to let a 35-year winning streak go against the USA. The last time the Eagles claimed a victory over the Red Roses was in the 1991 Rugby World Cup and since then England have won all 22 matches. The Red Roses got back to winning ways and, while their recent losses to Canada displayed the top sides had caught up with the world No 1 team, Friday’s outing against the USA evidenced that outside the top three there is still a gap to be closed.

The USA headed into the match at Sports Illustrated Stadium in Harrison, New Jersey, in good form with five consecutive wins, including victories over Wales and Ireland, and their No 8 Freda Tafuna has been one of the standouts across all of the teams during the WXV. However, England were able to contain the bright spark and, despite good performances from Alev Kelter and Hope Rogers, the hosts did not have enough firepower.

• Six clubs found to be balance-sheet insolvent

Prem Rugby clubs’ collective losses and debt levels are continuing to increase despite growing interest from global companies and financiers shown by the recent investment of Red Bull, Sir James Dyson, and the Black Knight group which owns AFC Bournemouth.

The third edition of the Leonard Curtis Rugby Finance Report published on Tuesday shows that the financial losses of the 10 Prem clubs rose from £34m to £36.5m over the 2024-25 season and combined debt levels increased from £342.5m to £366.1m, while the top flight’s total wage bills grew from £125.9m to £129.8m, 80% of revenues.

Tough does not remotely cover the job of the world’s best rugby referees and the lengths to which they go to navigate the sport’s labyrinthine laws

The 13th team participating at the Nations Championship this month are an intriguing bunch. If you didn’t know much about rugby and had wandered into a first-floor conference room at a hotel near Windsor on Monday you might almost have mistaken them for a gathering of airline pilots from nearby Heathrow. Slim, intelligent, studious … you’d trust them to stay calm on the flight deck.

Stick them in matchday kit, however, and the world’s top rugby union referees do not always enjoy universal respect, certainly online. They can be unflappably brilliant for 79 and a half minutes and yet still be defined by one hairline call barely visible to the naked eye. Every Test in which they are involved is an away game and, popularity wise, they often receive the same unconditional love as traffic wardens and the chancellor of the exchequer.

items.desc:
Financial success of the three-day finale in London later this month promises to make or break the concept

Guess how many people attended the recent Oktoberfest in Munich, the famous annual pilgrimage for people with a sense of fun and a collective thirst to quench? Admittedly the event spanned a fortnight but the figure is still pretty remarkable. There were 7.4m visitors – a record – with around a quarter of them travelling from overseas.

Now imagine even a tenth of that congregation coming together for a like-minded three-day festival in London. Endless access to quality beer, the chance to make instant new friends and, if desired, plenty of fancy dress options (lederhosen not compulsory). With top-quality sporting entertainment also on tap. Let’s hear it for Glastonbury’s oval-ball cousin: Ruckfest, if you will.

The players certainly have that as they begin their autumn campaign against Australia.

It actually makes me more confident in an England victory. They will have a siege mentality, just as they did against France in the Six Nations – they might not have won that match but it was the best performance of the campaign by some distance. items.title: Steve Borthwick’s England channel their rage to resemble finished article | Andy Bull
items.desc:
With his team rampant in their demolition of Australia, the head coach’s work seems to be paying dividends

So this is what they have been building behind Twickenham’s big black gates. After all these weeks in which England have seemed to always be a work in progress, Steve Borthwick finally wheeled out something that felt like a finished version of his team. No excuses, no apologies, no explanations, no talk about how young and inexperienced they are, no assurances that they are going to take the learnings. It was enthralling for their supporters and an ugly, bloody sight for the rest of the world. They were arrogant, imposing, and excellent. For everyone else, you guess, they are going to be hard to like and hell to play against.

It was a record victory, and a blue‑riband result against an Australian team who only recently beat the Springboks, and who are surely a lot better than England allowed them to be here. And if there were still plenty of little errors in the first 40 minutes – a couple of silly scrum penalties, a couple of shonky lineout throws to straighten up – it still added up to one of England’s better games since Borthwick took over as head coach; their best, for sure, since they beat New Zealand here this time last year. Heck, Borthwick even managed to crack a smile when it was all over.

items.title: Henry Pollock powers seven-try England to crushing victory against Australia
items.desc:
• England 45-22 Australia

  • George, Chessum and Heyes scored first-half tries

England had promised to do their talking on the field and so it came to pass. After a turbulent few days, this result was certainly a thumping riposte to newspaper reports that all is not well within the court of Steve Borthwick. If Australia had imagined they might encounter distracted, half-hearted hosts, this seven-try romp suggested the precise opposite.

Maybe Borthwick should commission the Times to write his motivational pre-match speeches every week. On this evidence the ­Wallabies have some massive issues to address but, equally, England were com­fortably the better, more energetic side. Further improvement will still be demanded, of course, but this record number of points against ­Australia was easily their most satisfying all-round outing of the calendar year to date. Their three defining Ds – defence, discipline and desire – were conspicuous throughout and, at long last, they are starting to trust their exciting attacking talent out wide.
